questions.q: What is the specific job of the NVIDIA driver, as distinct from the CUDA Toolkit?
options: It lets a container reach the host's GPU
It is a kernel-level module that lets the OS and hardware actually talk to the physical GPU
It compiles GPU-accelerated code written against the CUDA API
It schedules time-slicing between pods sharing one GPU
questions.explain: The driver is the kernel-level module that lets the OS recognize and communicate with the physical GPU hardware. The CUDA Toolkit is a separate, user-space layer on top of it.

questions.q: When nvidia-smi reports a "CUDA Version" field, what does that value actually represent?
options: The exact CUDA Toolkit version installed on the system
The version of the NVIDIA Container Toolkit in use
The Kubernetes device plugin version
The maximum CUDA version the installed driver can support, not necessarily what's installed
questions.explain: The driver and CUDA Toolkit are versioned independently. The CUDA Version shown by nvidia-smi is the upper bound the driver supports, thanks to NVIDIA's compatibility guarantees, not a report of what Toolkit version is actually installed.

questions.q: Why does a plain docker run on a GPU-equipped host fail to see the GPU without further configuration?
options: Containers are isolated from the host by default, including GPU device files and driver libraries
Docker does not support Linux hosts with GPUs attached
The NVIDIA driver must be reinstalled inside every container image
GPUs can only be accessed from virtual machines, never containers
questions.explain: Container isolation by default extends to GPU device files and driver libraries, so a container has no visibility into the host's GPU until something explicitly bridges that gap.

questions.q: What does the NVIDIA Container Toolkit actually do?
options: It replaces the CUDA Toolkit entirely
It installs a runtime hook that mounts the host's GPU devices and driver libraries into a container at start time
It is a Kubernetes-only component with no Docker equivalent
It installs the NVIDIA kernel driver on the host
questions.explain: The Container Toolkit installs a container runtime hook that, when a container starts, mounts the host's GPU device files and matching driver libraries into it — closing the isolation gap.

questions.q: What does running `sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker` accomplish?
options: It installs the NVIDIA GPU Operator
It partitions a physical GPU into MIG instances
It downloads the NVIDIA driver for the first time
It registers the NVIDIA runtime hook with the Docker daemon, so --gpus all actually works
questions.explain: Installing the Container Toolkit package alone isn't enough — nvidia-ctk runtime configure is the step that registers the NVIDIA runtime with Docker so it knows to use the hook when a container requests GPU access.
